He later pleaded guilty to those killings and is serving multiple life sentences without the possibility of parole at the Potosi Correctional Center in Missouri. Williams hopes that somebody out there remembers something that could help investigators determine what happened to Pamela. “​You know, she’s still missing, but she may be a victim in the serial case,” he said. “We need all [the] help and leads.” If anyone has information about Pamela Dalton’s whereabouts, please contact the Sikeston Department of Public Safety at 573-471-4711 or the Scott County Sheriff’s Office at 573-545-3525. Cheryl Scherer It has been more than 47 years since Cheryl Scherer, then 19, vanished from her job at the Rhodes Pump-Ur-Own gas station on April 17, 1979, in Scott City. Authorities believe she was abducted just before noon. Cheryl’s case is the oldest unsolved missing person case in Scott County. “Dateline” spoke with the Scott County Sheriff’s Office and Cheryl’s siblings about her disappearance in Season 5 of the “Dateline: Missing in America” podcast. Sister Diane Scherer-Morris told “Dateline” the family doesn’t believe Cheryl left the gas station on her own. “Never did it cross our minds,” she said. “She’s just not that kind of person. She just would not have done that.” Wheetley became the Scott County sheriff last year. He said he was familiar with Cheryl’s case. ​“It’s a case that’s been talked about a lot,” he told “Dateline.” “All the possibilities of theories and conspiracies have been talked about over time.” Williams, the detective sergeant, joined the case in 2021. Looking back at the initial investigation, Williams said, investigators “did everything that they could in that time period.” More than $400 was missing from the bank bag at the gas station. In recent years, authorities have used DNA testing in the hope of developing new leads. Williams said the testing identified as many as 30 possible DNA profiles on the bag. Investigators are still hopeful the DNA evidence could lead them in the right direction. The sheriff’s office conducted a large-scale excavation for Cheryl this year after eight cadaver dogs alerted to the possible presence of human remains in the same location. They didn’t find Cheryl, but investigators are determined to continue the search. “I use a lot of four-letter words, but ‘quit’ and ‘stop’ is not one of them,” Williams said. In the nearly half-century since Cheryl disappeared, her family has dedicated itself to bringing attention not only to Cheryl’s case, but also to the cases of other missing persons in the area. “Every missing person has a name, and they have a story. And everyone should be able to finish that story,” Diane said. When she disappeared, Cheryl Scherer was 5 feet, 1 inch tall and weighed 100 pounds, with blue eyes and shoulder-length red hair. She would be 67 years old this month. If you have any information about her case, please contact the Scott County Sheriff’s Office at 573-545-3525. If you have a story to share with “Dateline,” please submit it here.

articles.title: In 1964, a 27-year-old woman bought an abandoned 18 acre island off Maine and built a small house to live there alone; 22 years later the island was donated to become a wildlife sanctuary
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Before it was a wildlife sanctuary, it was a woman's abode. Witch Island is an approximately 18-acre land area off the coast of South Bristol, Maine, .
articles.body: Before it was a wildlife sanctuary, it was a woman's abode. Witch Island is an approximately 18-acre land area off the coast of South Bristol, Maine, United States. Named after the woman who used to live there, it was sold off to another who donated it to become a wildlife sanctuary, as per a report by Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust.The island's earliest known name was Stewart's, held by a settler whose identity dissolved into a rumour. Local lore claimed the pirate Dixey Bull once made his hideaway there in the 1630s, and a French and Indian War legend told of a corvette that ran aground nearby while fleeing a swifter British sloop. Ownership passed through the Gamage family of South Bristol before Captain Samuel H. Davis acquired it in 1830. Under his name, it became Davis Island, and the porgy boom of the 1860s brought fishermen to the surrounding waters in great numbers. When Davis died in 1884, a bitter family lawsuit over his will eventually sent the island to auction, and in 1887 it found new owners who would give it the name it carries still. Daniel and Anna Chittenden bought the island that autumn, intending to build a summer retreat. And Anna was no ordinary buyer.The Witch of Wall StreetBorn Anna Loomis in Ohio and raised amid the rough early years of Milwaukee, Anna's life before the island was already extraordinary. Married at fifteen to a gambler who beat her and squandered every fortune he made, she turned to the stage to escape poverty, performing under the name Grace Courtland and eventually running her own theatrical company. She survived the sinking of the steamship Idaho in 1878, famously cutting a lifeboat free with an axe when she sensed the disaster coming before it struck, a vision she said she'd had the very first night at sea. Divorced, remarried, and abandoned again, she reinvented herself once more, this time as a clairvoyant and financial seer.It was on Wall Street that she found her most enduring fame. So many of her predictions about stocks came true that financier James R. Keene supposedly crowned her the "Witch of Wall Street" after she called a trading session for him with uncanny accuracy. She counted bankers, brokers, and speculators among her clients, claimed to have exposed a stock-trading scheme built on secret bulletins about President Garfield's health, and published her own lecture excoriating the Wall Street monopolists of her day. But fame curdled into spectacle: by the 1880s she was a fixture of dime museums from Buffalo to Kansas City, billed alongside sideshow curiosities, dogged by family scandal, lawsuits, and imitators who stole her stage name outright.It was this same restless, theatrical woman who built a modest cottage among Witch Island's birches, waving a flag to passing boats to invite strangers ashore for a reading. A Boston journalist who visited in 1890 described the place as blanketed in birch trees, its owner both hermit and hostess. The nickname stuck to the land itself, and Davis Island quietly became Witch Island.From abode to wildlife sanctuaryThe Chittendens sold the island in 1916, and it passed to novelist Henry C. Rowland, whose family used it as a summer camp for decades, complete with an Airedale terrier, two pet seals, and a tame crow. After Rowland's widow and children eventually sold the property in 1964, it came into the hands of a woman who would decide its permanent fate, Jane Sewall.Sewall had loved the island since childhood, rowing around its shore as a seven-year-old and picnicking beneath its hardwoods with her family, who lived nearby. When the long-vacant island came up for sale, her sister later said Jane wanted it more than anything else in the world. She bought it in 1964, cleared the storm-battered old buildings, and built a small house of her own on its southern end, choosing to live there quietly, largely alone, for the better part of two decades.Sewall grew increasingly troubled by visitors who came to the island's beaches and left campfires smouldering behind them. She posted signs, first polite, then blunt, warning against fires. In letters to Maine newspapers, she pleaded for a kind of stewardship from strangers, asking people to tread lightly, to leave the wildflowers and birds undisturbed, to understand that an island's beauty survives only if those who visit it choose restraint over carelessness.In the late 1970s, Maine's tax laws for forested land shifted, threatening Sewall with a choice between costly penalties or ceding a portion of her island. In 1983, she released roughly a third of Witch Island to the Maine Coast Heritage Trust. Then, with new federal tax reforms approaching at the end of 1986, she made the larger decision that would define the island's future: she donated the entirety of Witch Island to the Maine Audubon Society, to be preserved forever as a wildlife sanctuary. She had spent years searching, she said, for an institution that would keep her island safe for good, one that would let her return to see it remain beautiful, even after it was no longer legally hers.The Maine Audubon Society managed the sanctuary for more than two decades before transferring its stewardship to the Damariscotta River Association in 2009. Following a 2019 merger, the association became the Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust. Today, Witch Island remains intentionally uninhabited under the trustâs care. Kayakers can reach its beaches, hikers can explore its half-mile of trails, and children attending science camps can learn about its plants and wildlife. The islandâs transformation from a private home into a protected sanctuary shows how preserving a special place can help protect it for future generations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Angélique Kidjo on making Hollywood Walk of Fame history: 'This star is for Africa'
articles.summary: The musical icon from Benin tells the BBC about why Africa and Africans are so important to music.
articles.body:
Five-time Grammy award winner Angélique Kidjo, who made history on Tuesday to become the first African musician to get a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, has told the BBC she wants to dedicate the accolade to the continent of her birth.

"This star is for all the continent of Africa. Because if I was not African, would I be here?" said the 66-year-old musical icon from Benin.

She reiterated her message, made at the ceremony in Los Angeles to mark her four-decade career, about the importance of Africans to the world of music.

"Without the blues brought by the slaves in America, there's no R&B, there's no rock and roll, there's no soul music, there's no jazz. All of it comes from Africa."

Angélique Kidjo's secret to success: Being hangry

Kidjo told BBC Focus on Africa TV that Africans themselves needed to appreciate what they had given the world, and nurture talent at home.

"Let's celebrate our artists in their own right on the continent. Let's give them visibility, strength, because music creates economy," she said.

Most African artists - besides mega stars who have a global fanbase - struggle to make a living as they rarely get paid the royalties they are owed.

"We need to recognise our artists and create a system for them to make money on their continent and to participate also in creating jobs."

As her illustrious career was immortalised in Los Angeles, Kidjo became emotional - wiping away tears.

"At that moment, I'm like, dad, mum, I wish you were here with me to see [this]" the songstress explained to the BBC.

"I couldn't take the emotion. They were not here to taste the fruit of what they've created. How they have nurtured my curiosity, my love for music."

Kidjo - who has taken African sounds to global audiences, blending influences from home with funk, jazz and pop - grew up in Benin and then went to Paris aged 23, citing oppression from the country's then-communist government.

At her Walk of Fame ceremony, she was joined by other family, friends and stars such as Hollywood actors Willem Dafoe and Djimon Hounsou, who is also from Benin, and Nigerian musician Adekunle Gold.

The gathering was filled with singing and dancing in celebration of her career, which has included collaborations with big names such as Burna Boy, John Legend, Bono and Alicia Keys.

Her latest album, HOPE!!, was released earlier this year with tracks produced by Pharrell Williams, and collaborations with Ayra Starr, Quavo, Nile Rogers and Diane Warren.

Kidjo has released 18 albums in total and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards, which she has won five times.

She also won the 2023 Polar Music Prize, and two years earlier was named as one of Time's 100 Most Influential People.

"She is without a doubt the hardest working woman in showbusiness," Dafoe said at the ceremony.

"The first time I saw Angélique perform live, I thought her music, her dancing, her commitment were incredible."

The Spider-Man star likened her energy to that of soul singer James Brown, who he called the "hardest working man in showbusiness".

"She's not only an incredible performer... songwriter and musician, but also an incredibly kind and giving person and a real deal activist."

Kidjo is a Unicef and Oxfam goodwill ambassador, and is the co-founder of the Batonga Foundation, which helps vulnerable young girls and women in Benin.

At the Los Angeles gathering she was also praised by Harvey Mason Jr, the CEO of Recording Academy - the organisation that also oversees the Grammy awards.

"She's connected cultures, she's crossed borders, she's reminded audiences everywhere that while we may come from different backgrounds, her music unites in a way that few other things can," he said.

During her interview with the BBC, the musician's phone kept ringing with those wanting to congratulate her.

"Yesterday I received the call of the president of Benin," she said.

"Today I received the call of Chris Blackwell, the founder of Island Records, the producer of Bob Marley, the maker of U2 and so on and so forth."

Kidjo explained how fundamental Blackwell, who signed her in the 1990s, had been to her success - launching her breakthrough album Logozo.

"I said to him at that moment… 'Can I do the music I want to do and keep my cultural identity without anyone imposing any other music on my shoulder?' He said… 'It's no brainer.'"

Kidjo joins Charlize Theron, a white South African actress, in representing Africa on the Walk of Fame, which comprises more than 2,800 stars.

She said she was amazed to hear a year ago that she had been nominated for a Hollywood star, telling Focus on Africa she did not believe the news given to her by her husband until she said she had seen it on the BBC.

And when asked about the significance of becoming the first African musician with a star, she replied: "Changes that last take time."

articles.title: Nicole Kidman empezó a hacerse dermaplaning porque pensaba que era "como afeitarse" y ahora dice que nota mejor sus cosméticos
articles.summary: Rachel Keys, enfermera experta en dermocosmética, explica qué hay de cierto en esa sensación y cuándo este tratamiento puede convertirse en un problema
articles.body:
Nicole Kidman lleva décadas cambiando de piel delante de una cámara. Pelucas, prótesis, maquillaje, transformaciones físicas y personajes en los que cuesta reconocerla. Pero cuando se apagan los focos, la actriz parece buscar justo lo contrario: sentirse ella misma. A sus 59 años, esa relación con su imagen también ha cambiado y, en una reciente entrevista con Allure , ha contado uno de los últimos gestos que ha incorporado a su rutina de belleza: el dermaplaning .

"Empecé a hacerlo hace aproximadamente un año", explica Kidman, que reconoce que durante mucho tiempo tuvo reparos porque pensaba que era "como afeitarse". Ahora asegura que nota que su hidratante se aplica con más facilidad y también los sérums que utiliza. Siente que consigue una exfoliación natural.

La experiencia de la actriz plantea una pregunta bastante más interesante que copiar o no su rutina: ¿realmente los cosméticos funcionan mejor después de un dermaplaning o simplemente parece que lo hacen? Rachel Keys, enfermera experta en dermocosmética, aclara que hay una diferencia importante entre ambas cosas.

El 'dermaplaning' de Nicole Kidman no es simplemente "afeitarse la cara"

Es normal que se relacione porque se parecen. En ambos casos hay una cuchilla involucrada que pasa sobre la superficie cutánea y elimina el vello fino. Pero eso es todo lo que tienen en común. "El dermaplaning es, básicamente, una exfoliación superficial que se realiza con una cuchilla específica y estéril. Además de retirar el vello fino de la cara, elimina células muertas de la capa más superficial de la piel", explica Rachel Keys.

Ese segundo efecto es el que marca la diferencia. Mientras que al afeitar el rostro en casa el objetivo principal suele ser retirar el vello, con el dermaplaning se busca también trabajar la textura cutánea mediante una exfoliación mecánica superficial. Al eliminar parte de las células acumuladas y el vello fino, la superficie queda más uniforme y suave . Y esa nueva textura cambia también cómo sentimos cualquier producto que aplicamos después.

Por qué Nicole Kidman nota que sus sérums funcionan mejor después del 'dermaplaning'

Que un sérum se deslice mejor o parezca integrarse de manera diferente sobre la piel no significa necesariamente que sus principios activos hayan multiplicado su eficacia. " Estamos dejando una superficie mucho más lisa . Al retirar el vello y parte de las células acumuladas, el sérum o la crema se deslizan mejor y se reparten de una forma más uniforme", explica Keys. De ahí esa sensación inmediata de "piel nueva" , más suave y luminosa, que puede hacer que percibamos incluso nuestros cosméticos habituales de otra manera.

¿Penetran más? La experta pide prudencia. "Puede facilitar ligeramente el contacto de los productos con la piel , pero no diría que el dermaplaning hace que todos los activos penetren mucho más ". Es decir, Nicole Kidman no se equivoca cuando dice que nota mejor la aplicación de sus hidratantes y sérums. Lo que es incorrecto es convertir esa experiencia sensorial en la promesa de que cualquier principio activo va a funcionar más por haber pasado antes una cuchilla por el rostro. "No debemos pensar que, por hacernos dermaplaning , un sérum va a multiplicar su eficacia" , resume Keys.

El 'dermaplaning' de Nicole Kidman no es una buena idea para todas las pieles

Que una actriz diga que algo le funciona no convierte ese tratamiento en universal. Según Keys, puede ser especialmente interesante cuando existe bastante vello facial fino , una textura irregular o esa apariencia apagada que muchas veces buscamos corregir mediante exfoliación. Sin embargo, hay pieles en las que retirar mecánicamente la capa más superficial puede conseguir justo el efecto contrario al deseado .

"Si tenemos una piel muy sensible, rosácea, dermatitis , acné inflamatorio o la barrera cutánea está irritada, podemos provocar más rojez y sensibilidad", advierte. Su recomendación en esas circunstancias es primero recuperar la piel y después plantearse exfoliarla. La barrera cutánea irritada no necesita que hagamos más cosas; en muchas ocasiones necesita que dejemos de hacerlas. La exfoliación, además, no tiene una única forma. Existen alternativas químicas y enzimáticas con mecanismos diferentes, y su elección debe adaptarse al estado y las necesidades de la piel.

Cada cuánto hacer el dermaplaning de Nicole Kidman y qué no ponerse después

Otro error sería interpretar una piel más lisa como una invitación a repetir el tratamiento continuamente. Keys sitúa una frecuencia orientativa de una vez cada tres o cuatro semanas , siempre condicionada a que la piel lo tolere correctamente.

Pero casi más importante que lo que hacemos durante el dermaplaning es lo que hacemos después. "Me olvidaría durante unos días de hacer cosas a la piel: nada de exfoliantes, retinoides ni ácidos potentes", recomienda la experta. Tras una exfoliación de este tipo, propone volver a lo básico con una rutina hidratante y calmante. Y hay un producto que no admite negociación: fotoprotector SPF 50 todos los días. " La piel recién exfoliada agradece mucho más la calma que una sobredosis de activos", sentencia Keys.

Lo que sí puede hacer que tus cosméticos penetren mejor

Una cosa es que un cosmético se deslice mejor después del dermaplaning y otra que esté formulado para conseguir que sus activos lleguen más lejos. La cosmética más avanzada ya trabaja precisamente en esto, buscando formas de atravesarla o modularla de manera controlada.

Entre las tecnologías que más están dando que hablar están los liposomas, que encapsulan los activos para protegerlos y favorecer su distribución; las moléculas de bajo peso molecular; las microagujas cosméticas o espículas ; y la Keratinasa PB333 , una enzima obtenida mediante ingeniería genética que crea pequeñas vías de paso entre las células más superficiales sin comprometer la función protectora de la piel.

Esta última la he probado personalmente en las monodosis de SmartKer, igual que los sérums con microagujas cosméticas, y son dos tecnologías que me han resultado especialmente interesantes porque están pensadas para aplicar en formato sérum solas o antes de tus productos habituales ya que son capaces de ayudar a la penetración de los ingredientes de estos.

Como explica el químico y doctor en Nanomedicina Arturo Álvarez-Bautista, la nueva cosmética busca "aumentar la biodisponibilidad" y aumentar su permanencia en la piel.
paragraphs: Nicole Kidman lleva décadas cambiando de piel delante de una cámara. Pelucas, prótesis, maquillaje, transformaciones físicas y personajes en los que cuesta reconocerla. Pero cuando se apagan los focos, la actriz parece buscar justo lo contrario: sentirse ella misma. A sus 59 años, esa relación con su imagen también ha cambiado y, en una reciente entrevista con Allure , ha contado uno de los últimos gestos que ha incorporado a su rutina de belleza: el dermaplaning .

"Empecé a hacerlo hace aproximadamente un año", explica Kidman, que reconoce que durante mucho tiempo tuvo reparos porque pensaba que era "como afeitarse". Ahora asegura que nota que su hidratante se aplica con más facilidad y también los sérums que utiliza. Siente que consigue una exfoliación natural.

La experiencia de la actriz plantea una pregunta bastante más interesante que copiar o no su rutina: ¿realmente los cosméticos funcionan mejor después de un dermaplaning o simplemente parece que lo hacen? Rachel Keys, enfermera experta en dermocosmética, aclara que hay una diferencia importante entre ambas cosas.
El 'dermaplaning' de Nicole Kidman no es simplemente "afeitarse la cara"

Es normal que se relacione porque se parecen. En ambos casos hay una cuchilla involucrada que pasa sobre la superficie cutánea y elimina el vello fino. Pero eso es todo lo que tienen en común. "El dermaplaning es, básicamente, una exfoliación superficial que se realiza con una cuchilla específica y estéril. Además de retirar el vello fino de la cara, elimina células muertas de la capa más superficial de la piel", explica Rachel Keys.

Ese segundo efecto es el que marca la diferencia. Mientras que al afeitar el rostro en casa el objetivo principal suele ser retirar el vello, con el dermaplaning se busca también trabajar la textura cutánea mediante una exfoliación mecánica superficial. Al eliminar parte de las células acumuladas y el vello fino, la superficie queda más uniforme y suave . Y esa nueva textura cambia también cómo sentimos cualquier producto que aplicamos después.
Por qué Nicole Kidman nota que sus sérums funcionan mejor después del 'dermaplaning'

Que un sérum se deslice mejor o parezca integrarse de manera diferente sobre la piel no significa necesariamente que sus principios activos hayan multiplicado su eficacia. " Estamos dejando una superficie mucho más lisa . Al retirar el vello y parte de las células acumuladas, el sérum o la crema se deslizan mejor y se reparten de una forma más uniforme", explica Keys. De ahí esa sensación inmediata de "piel nueva" , más suave y luminosa, que puede hacer que percibamos incluso nuestros cosméticos habituales de otra manera.

¿Penetran más? La experta pide prudencia. "Puede facilitar ligeramente el contacto de los productos con la piel , pero no diría que el dermaplaning hace que todos los activos penetren mucho más ". Es decir, Nicole Kidman no se equivoca cuando dice que nota mejor la aplicación de sus hidratantes y sérums. Lo que es incorrecto es convertir esa experiencia sensorial en la promesa de que cualquier principio activo va a funcionar más por haber pasado antes una cuchilla por el rostro. "No debemos pensar que, por hacernos dermaplaning , un sérum va a multiplicar su eficacia" , resume Keys.
El 'dermaplaning' de Nicole Kidman no es una buena idea para todas las pieles

Que una actriz diga que algo le funciona no convierte ese tratamiento en universal. Según Keys, puede ser especialmente interesante cuando existe bastante vello facial fino , una textura irregular o esa apariencia apagada que muchas veces buscamos corregir mediante exfoliación. Sin embargo, hay pieles en las que retirar mecánicamente la capa más superficial puede conseguir justo el efecto contrario al deseado .

"Si tenemos una piel muy sensible, rosácea, dermatitis , acné inflamatorio o la barrera cutánea está irritada, podemos provocar más rojez y sensibilidad", advierte. Su recomendación en esas circunstancias es primero recuperar la piel y después plantearse exfoliarla. La barrera cutánea irritada no necesita que hagamos más cosas; en muchas ocasiones necesita que dejemos de hacerlas. La exfoliación, además, no tiene una única forma. Existen alternativas químicas y enzimáticas con mecanismos diferentes, y su elección debe adaptarse al estado y las necesidades de la piel.
Cada cuánto hacer el dermaplaning de Nicole Kidman y qué no ponerse después

Otro error sería interpretar una piel más lisa como una invitación a repetir el tratamiento continuamente. Keys sitúa una frecuencia orientativa de una vez cada tres o cuatro semanas , siempre condicionada a que la piel lo tolere correctamente.

Pero casi más importante que lo que hacemos durante el dermaplaning es lo que hacemos después. "Me olvidaría durante unos días de hacer cosas a la piel: nada de exfoliantes, retinoides ni ácidos potentes", recomienda la experta. Tras una exfoliación de este tipo, propone volver a lo básico con una rutina hidratante y calmante. Y hay un producto que no admite negociación: fotoprotector SPF 50 todos los días. " La piel recién exfoliada agradece mucho más la calma que una sobredosis de activos", sentencia Keys.
Lo que sí puede hacer que tus cosméticos penetren mejor

Una cosa es que un cosmético se deslice mejor después del dermaplaning y otra que esté formulado para conseguir que sus activos lleguen más lejos. La cosmética más avanzada ya trabaja precisamente en esto, buscando formas de atravesarla o modularla de manera controlada.

Entre las tecnologías que más están dando que hablar están los liposomas, que encapsulan los activos para protegerlos y favorecer su distribución; las moléculas de bajo peso molecular; las microagujas cosméticas o espículas ; y la Keratinasa PB333 , una enzima obtenida mediante ingeniería genética que crea pequeñas vías de paso entre las células más superficiales sin comprometer la función protectora de la piel.

Esta última la he probado personalmente en las monodosis de SmartKer, igual que los sérums con microagujas cosméticas, y son dos tecnologías que me han resultado especialmente interesantes porque están pensadas para aplicar en formato sérum solas o antes de tus productos habituales ya que son capaces de ayudar a la penetración de los ingredientes de estos.
Como explica el químico y doctor en Nanomedicina Arturo Álvarez-Bautista, la nueva cosmética busca "aumentar la biodisponibilidad" y aumentar su permanencia en la piel.

articles.title: Residents in Conwy remove Greenpeace Andy Burnham mountain mural
articles.summary: After wildfires the group painted an image bearing the words "Our house is on fire, Andy".
articles.body:
Residents affected by wildfires say they were left "angry and upset" after a mural of Prime Minister Andy Burnham was painted on a blackened mountainside above their homes.

Dubbing it an "intrusion into grief" two walkers removed Greenpeace's work with rakes.

The campaign group's 1,120-sq-m anti-oil and drilling image showed Burnham holding an oil drum and the words: "Our house is on fire Andy."

Greenpeace said the work, in Capelulo, Conwy, had not been meant to upset people but to "draw attention to the escalating climate crisis".

In July about 200 acres of land was affected by wildfires with North Wales Fire and Rescue Service declaring it a major incident .

The blaze came within yards of destroying properties - with 36 homes evacuated .

Hairdresser Allie Evans was among those who had to leave.

When pictures of Greenpeace's mural emerged on Monday she went up the mountain to see it.

The 53-year-old said: "I can't remember having been so angry and upset all at once.

"It was so disrespectful to the landscapes. It was also an intrusion into local grief, which is how we felt when we came back home to see the mountain so utterly changed.

"It added insult to injury. I couldn't understand how an organisation that wants to protect the environment, can graffiti the earth and stain rocks which are millions of years old."

A banner would have delivered Greenpeace's message just as easily, without affecting the environment, Evans said.

She and Rhos-on-Sea resident, Dean Ward, went to remove the paint.

Evans said: "We were concerned a lot of people would want to go up the mountain to see the graffiti, and the hillside would get trashed."

She said Greenpeace had painted over rocks and soil, staining them.

"Had we not done anything, it would have been there for a long time," Evans said.

The pair had broken up the paint and raked flakes into the soil, but Evans said some parts were "baked" so it had been difficult to do so.

"So you can still see stripes on the site, if not the overall graffiti."

Ward told Greenpeace online he had taken "great pleasure" in removing its work, adding: "Thought Greenpeace was all about leave no trace and you do this to the mountain side."

Bangor Conwy Môn Senedd member, Janet Finch-Saunders, accused the group of "environmental vandalism", saying burnt hillsides should not be used "as a canvas for political protest".

Greenpeace UK's co-executive director, Areeba Hamid, said: "Our artwork was not intended to disturb [people's] grief but to draw attention to the escalating climate crisis that's putting these beautiful places and communities at risk.

"We took great care to minimise our impact on the land. The artwork was temporary by design: created with a water-based paint often used on sports turf and safe for grass, plants and soil.

"It was applied to an area where the fire had already burned away all living vegetation, leaving just rocks and ash."

The threat, Hamid said, had not been "a dab of water-based paint" but "extreme weather driven by fossil fuels".

She added: "We wanted to challenge the system that caused this damage and send a vital message to the prime minister: the science shows that more oil and gas drilling means more communities left to cope with the devastation brought by heat, droughts and wildfires."

articles.title: In 1994, Steve and Terri Irwin bought 3,500 acres to restore dwindling koala habitat, then planted 44,000 eucalyptus trees and added 1,630 more acres
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Steve and Terri Irwin transformed 3,500 acres into a thriving koala habitat at Ironbark Station, including planting 44,000 eucalyptus trees and expanding their conservation efforts significantly. Learn about the ongoing impact of their legacy on wildlife protection and habitat restoration.
articles.body: In 1994, Steve and Terri Irwin made a conservation investment that began with a simple idea: if koalas were losing habitat, protecting the animals alone would not be enough. That year, Australia Zoo bought 3,500 acres at Blackbutt in Queensland and named it Ironbark Station.According to Australia Zoo, Ironbark Station was purchased in 1994 to restore dwindling koala habitat and help increase koala numbers. Steve and Terri Irwin began the project by planting 44,000 eucalyptus trees, creating the foundation for a long-term habitat restoration effort. The conservation area was later expanded, allowing the project to protect a larger stretch of land and provide more space for recovering koala habitat.Rebuilding the trees koalas needFor koalas, a forest is more than cover. Eucalyptus trees provide the leaves that form the bulk of koalas' diet, while connected vegetation allows them to move between feeding and sheltering sites. That makes the Irwins' decision to plant thousands of eucalyptus trees especially significant. But putting trees into the ground is only the first stage of habitat restoration. Young trees need to survive long enough to become part of a functioning woodland, while weeds, fire, grazing and other pressures can determine whether restoration succeeds.Research in south-east Queensland has shown that the way remaining forest is distributed can influence koala habitat use. According to Biological Conservation, a study of koalas in a fragmented rural-urban landscape found that both the amount of forest and its spatial arrangement were associated with koala occurrence. The researchers also found that koalas were less likely to use isolated habitat patches and that movement between patches could expose them to hazards associated with crossing open or developed areas. These findings provide useful context for restoration efforts such as those at Ironbark Station. Replanting trees across a fragmented landscape can help expand existing habitat and, where plantings reconnect separated patches, potentially improve the continuity of vegetation available to koalas.Restoration can also benefit the wider landscape beyond the trees themselves. As native vegetation becomes established, it can provide shelter and feeding opportunities for other species while helping rebuild ecological connections between previously degraded areas. For koalas, the long-term value of such work depends on whether planted trees survive and develop into a healthy, connected habitat that can continue supporting wildlife over time.More land, more restorationAustralia Zoo also notes that Ironbark Station was later expanded by an additional 1,630 acres for wildlife conservation, increasing the land available for habitat protection and restoration. The work has also involved tackling invasive plants and weeds that restrict native wildlife from moving freely in search of food and shelter, leaving koalas more vulnerable to feral animals. Because much of the terrain is difficult to access, removing the vegetation has required specialised equipment and continued over many years rather than being a one-time clearance effort. This approach also aligns with Australia's national guidance on koala habitat restoration. The environment department identifies habitat loss, fragmentation and degradation as major threats and recommends restoring habitat in ways that improve both its quality and connectivity. It also stresses that successful revegetation should account for local conditions and the ecological needs of koalas.The restoration is therefore aimed at more than simply increasing the amount of protected land. By reconnecting areas of native vegetation and reducing barriers created by weeds, the project can create a more continuous landscape through which koalas and other native animals can move. Over time, the return of native vegetation can also provide additional food and shelter, helping the restored areas function as habitat rather than isolated patches of surviving bushland.A project that continued after Steve IrwinSteve Irwin died in 2006, but the conservation work associated with his family continued to expand. Ironbark Station became part of a much larger network of conservation properties managed by Australia Zoo and Wildlife Warriors. Australia Zoo reports that the organisations now protect more than 450,000 acres of habitat across Queensland. Among the largest is the 330,000-acre Steve Irwin Wildlife Reserve on Cape York, which protects a diverse landscape of rainforest, wetlands and savannah. Together, these properties have extended the family's conservation efforts far beyond the original Ironbark Station.The project also reflected a broader shift in the familyâs conservation approach, from protecting individual animals to safeguarding the habitats they depend on. By acquiring and managing large areas of land, Australia Zoo and Wildlife Warriors could address threats such as habitat loss and fragmentation at a landscape scale. In this sense, Ironbark Station became part of a longer-term strategy in which restoring habitat was treated as essential to giving native wildlife a better chance of surviving in the wild.Ironbark Station ultimately shows that conservation is not always about dramatic interventions or immediate results. By restoring degraded land and protecting it over the long term, the project created the conditions for native vegetation and koala habitat to recover. What began as an effort to plant trees became a broader attempt to rebuild a functioning ecosystem, demonstrating that effective conservation can depend as much on patience, protection and continuity as on the work of putting trees in the ground.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rosenberg: Shortage of petrol but not patriotism as Russians feel growing impact of war
articles.summary: Drivers are waiting hours in fuel queues, as Moscow prepares to celebrate Russian Flag Day.
articles.body:
At a petrol station in the south-east of Moscow, Svyatoslav has been queuing in his car for two hours.

The sign board up ahead has just been changed to show there's no fuel.

"They say there will be petrol here," Svyatoslav tells me optimistically. "They just don't know when. Maybe today, maybe tomorrow."

I ask him why he doesn't drive off and look for another place to fill up.

"I haven't got enough in the tank to do that," Svyatoslav replies.

Even if he had, there'd be no quick fuel fix for Svyatoslav. This week across Moscow, and in other parts of Russia, there have been long queues for petrol.

"Unscheduled repairs at oil refineries," explain Russian officials.

Those repairs have been triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. Such long-range attacks sparked major fuel shortages earlier this summer. The targeting of oil refineries has continued apace.

This time the queues in Moscow are even longer than before. The authorities appear to be struggling to resolve problems with refining capacity and logistics.

"The second wave of the fuel crisis is building," declared broadsheet Nezavisimaya Gazeta this week.

Driving around Moscow this week two things catch the eye: patriotic announcements on giant billboards about Russian Flag Day…and giant petrol queues.

Outside one Moscow petrol station I count 80 vehicles waiting in line.

The search for fuel is now a constant struggle.

"Last night I went to get petrol at 11pm," says Elizaveta who's queuing again for fuel. "By midnight I'd reached the front of the queue. Then they shut the petrol station until 2am."

"I drove into Moscow yesterday from the provinces," says Lyubov. "It was empty petrol stations all the way."

To stay calm in the queue Lyubov is stroking her pet dog Agatha.

"Everyone says there is a difficult situation in the country," Lyubov tells me. "Everyone connects this to that situation."

Before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 there were no drone attacks on Russian oil refineries - or on any facilities inside Russia. These strikes haven't forced the Kremlin to U-turn. It's continuing what it still calls the "special military operation", Russia's war on Ukraine.

To ease the crisis, Russia has begun importing petrol.

That is extraordinary for a country widely recognised as an energy superpower and one of the world's leading exporters of crude oil.

To reduce the fuel shortage the government has also temporarily authorised the production and sale of lower-grade petrol, like Euro 2, which is faster to produce. Euro 2 contains up to 50 times more sulphur than modern Euro 5 and was banned in Russia in 2013.

"For modern cars," wrote the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta, "regular use of lower-grade petrol can increase the pressure on the fuel injector, spark plugs, oxygen sensors, the catalytic converter and soot filter. Euro 2 won't kill an engine on one re-fuelling. But it sharply reduces the margin of safety."

It's not just the targeting of oil facilities which have brought the war home to Russians.

Ukrainian strikes on distribution centres of Wildberries, Russia's equivalent of Amazon, are causing disruption to shoppers and economic pain for sellers.

This week President Vladimir Putin conceded that attacks on industrial facilities and infrastructure "do inflict damage; this is obvious. We understand this, we see it."

But the Kremlin leader played down the problems.

"There are no critical consequences from such attacks. There have not been and cannot be."

"It is a disconnect between people's feelings and the description of reality by Vladimir Putin, the description of his personal reality in his head," believes Andrei Kolesnikov, a columnist for independent news outlet Novaya Gazeta.

"Maybe he's trying to hypnotise himself that everything is okay."

Recent polling inside Russia, including by the Public Opinion Foundation, suggest that anxiety in society is rising. That would suggest that the Kremlin's message of 'keep calm and carry on' isn't landing.

"This permanent feeling of anxiety is with everyone right now. You feel that something is wrong. Anxiety is the main sentiment," says Kolesnikov.

"This regime doesn't demonstrate any model of the future: the nearest future, a middle- term future, a long-term future. We are 'great' right now. What are the qualities of this greatness? The petrol crisis? In that sense, the future is aborted. People are trying not to think about the future. The horizon of planning is very short."

A few minutes' drive from the petrol station where I'd been chatting with Svyatoslav, I spot another long queue.

The local authorities have set up stalls and put on a street concert to mark Russian Flag Day.

There may be a shortage of petrol. But not of patriotism. Not here.

"It's my country, my fate, my dream," croons a singer. "I'm raising my flag. The flag of my country."

Volunteers are handing out Russian tricolours to people on the square.

"Dear friends, we live in a wonderful country!" declares one of the speakers. "We know that we will always be victorious. I wish you peaceful skies, a good mood, comfort, prosperity and pride in our country."

Along with the candyfloss there are Kalashnikovs. At one stall children are being shown an array of military hardware, including hand-held rocket launchers. The kids are picking up the weapons and posing with them.

It hints to the growing militarisation of Russian society.

The patriotic presentation is lifting some people's spirits.

"Difficulties unite us," pensioner Tatyana tells me. "The harder things are, the stronger we get."

But the war is very much on people's minds - especially the Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region.

"When you go to sleep you don't know if you'll wake up in the morning," Angelina tells me. "That's the only problem. Everything else is fine."

"The problems we have are high prices, petrol shortages and last night, for the first time, my windows shook…I heard 'boom boom!' another woman tells me.

"Right now, it's important to take care of your psychological state, so that it's strong and unbreakable. So that, whatever happens, you can say: 'Oh well, never mind.'

Comments like that suggest that Russians don't believe they can influence what's happening around them. All they feel they can do is try to adapt.
paragraphs: At a petrol station in the south-east of Moscow, Svyatoslav has been queuing in his car for two hours.
The sign board up ahead has just been changed to show there's no fuel.
"They say there will be petrol here," Svyatoslav tells me optimistically. "They just don't know when. Maybe today, maybe tomorrow."
I ask him why he doesn't drive off and look for another place to fill up.
"I haven't got enough in the tank to do that," Svyatoslav replies.
Even if he had, there'd be no quick fuel fix for Svyatoslav. This week across Moscow, and in other parts of Russia, there have been long queues for petrol.
"Unscheduled repairs at oil refineries," explain Russian officials.

Those repairs have been triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. Such long-range attacks sparked major fuel shortages earlier this summer. The targeting of oil refineries has continued apace.
This time the queues in Moscow are even longer than before. The authorities appear to be struggling to resolve problems with refining capacity and logistics.
"The second wave of the fuel crisis is building," declared broadsheet Nezavisimaya Gazeta this week.
Driving around Moscow this week two things catch the eye: patriotic announcements on giant billboards about Russian Flag Day…and giant petrol queues.
Outside one Moscow petrol station I count 80 vehicles waiting in line.
The search for fuel is now a constant struggle.
"Last night I went to get petrol at 11pm," says Elizaveta who's queuing again for fuel. "By midnight I'd reached the front of the queue. Then they shut the petrol station until 2am."
"I drove into Moscow yesterday from the provinces," says Lyubov. "It was empty petrol stations all the way."
To stay calm in the queue Lyubov is stroking her pet dog Agatha.
"Everyone says there is a difficult situation in the country," Lyubov tells me. "Everyone connects this to that situation."

Before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 there were no drone attacks on Russian oil refineries - or on any facilities inside Russia. These strikes haven't forced the Kremlin to U-turn. It's continuing what it still calls the "special military operation", Russia's war on Ukraine.
To ease the crisis, Russia has begun importing petrol.
That is extraordinary for a country widely recognised as an energy superpower and one of the world's leading exporters of crude oil.

To reduce the fuel shortage the government has also temporarily authorised the production and sale of lower-grade petrol, like Euro 2, which is faster to produce. Euro 2 contains up to 50 times more sulphur than modern Euro 5 and was banned in Russia in 2013.

"For modern cars," wrote the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta, "regular use of lower-grade petrol can increase the pressure on the fuel injector, spark plugs, oxygen sensors, the catalytic converter and soot filter. Euro 2 won't kill an engine on one re-fuelling. But it sharply reduces the margin of safety."
It's not just the targeting of oil facilities which have brought the war home to Russians.
Ukrainian strikes on distribution centres of Wildberries, Russia's equivalent of Amazon, are causing disruption to shoppers and economic pain for sellers.
This week President Vladimir Putin conceded that attacks on industrial facilities and infrastructure "do inflict damage; this is obvious. We understand this, we see it."
But the Kremlin leader played down the problems.
"There are no critical consequences from such attacks. There have not been and cannot be."

"It is a disconnect between people's feelings and the description of reality by Vladimir Putin, the description of his personal reality in his head," believes Andrei Kolesnikov, a columnist for independent news outlet Novaya Gazeta.
"Maybe he's trying to hypnotise himself that everything is okay."

Recent polling inside Russia, including by the Public Opinion Foundation, suggest that anxiety in society is rising. That would suggest that the Kremlin's message of 'keep calm and carry on' isn't landing.
"This permanent feeling of anxiety is with everyone right now. You feel that something is wrong. Anxiety is the main sentiment," says Kolesnikov.

"This regime doesn't demonstrate any model of the future: the nearest future, a middle- term future, a long-term future. We are 'great' right now. What are the qualities of this greatness? The petrol crisis? In that sense, the future is aborted. People are trying not to think about the future. The horizon of planning is very short."
A few minutes' drive from the petrol station where I'd been chatting with Svyatoslav, I spot another long queue.
The local authorities have set up stalls and put on a street concert to mark Russian Flag Day.
There may be a shortage of petrol. But not of patriotism. Not here.
"It's my country, my fate, my dream," croons a singer. "I'm raising my flag. The flag of my country."
Volunteers are handing out Russian tricolours to people on the square.

"Dear friends, we live in a wonderful country!" declares one of the speakers. "We know that we will always be victorious. I wish you peaceful skies, a good mood, comfort, prosperity and pride in our country."

Along with the candyfloss there are Kalashnikovs. At one stall children are being shown an array of military hardware, including hand-held rocket launchers. The kids are picking up the weapons and posing with them.
It hints to the growing militarisation of Russian society.
The patriotic presentation is lifting some people's spirits.
"Difficulties unite us," pensioner Tatyana tells me. "The harder things are, the stronger we get."
But the war is very much on people's minds - especially the Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region.
"When you go to sleep you don't know if you'll wake up in the morning," Angelina tells me. "That's the only problem. Everything else is fine."
"The problems we have are high prices, petrol shortages and last night, for the first time, my windows shook…I heard 'boom boom!' another woman tells me.
"Right now, it's important to take care of your psychological state, so that it's strong and unbreakable. So that, whatever happens, you can say: 'Oh well, never mind.'
Comments like that suggest that Russians don't believe they can influence what's happening around them. All they feel they can do is try to adapt.

articles.title: Sydney Marathon medal wrongly features Munich stadium
articles.summary: Online sleuths detected the error after Sydney Marathon unveiled the double-sided medal.
articles.body:
One week out from the world-renowned Sydney Marathon, organisers face questions about whether designers etched the wrong city's stadium on the participation medal.

The medal appears to feature a stadium carved in the likeness of Allianz Arena in the German city of Munich, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney – which the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course runs past.

The BBC has reached out to Sydney Marathon for comment.

Some 40,000 runners will be taking part in the event on 30 August, after more than 120,000 ballot entries.

Speculation about a possible mix-up began after Sydney Marathon's official social media account unveiled its design for the 2026 medal, inviting users to "look closely and you'll find the story of the course in the details".

They continued: "A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way - starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House."

Munich's Allianz Arena is sculpted by thousands of diamond-shaped inflatable cushions, while Sydney's similarly-named Allianz Stadium has a flatter façade smoothed with long bronze fins.

The other face of the double-sided medal features a gold and indigo pattern designed by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian. Forty-two half-round markings lining the circular edge "represent each kilometre of the course", organisers explained.

Killian told the BBC he was not responsible for the other artwork.

The blunder follows a similar incident at last year's Great North Run in Newcastle, where medals mistakenly featured the Sunderland and Wear River – which is not part of the event.

Sydney was announced as the seventh city added to the Abbott majors series in 2024, joining London, Berlin, Boston, Chicago, New York, and Tokyo. Cape Town is set to become the eighth city when it hosts its first marathon major next year.

Great North Run medals show wrong city and river

articles.title: Iran-linked hackers behind cyber attack that shut down power plant, reports say
articles.summary: The government says at no point was there a risk to the UK's energy system during the attack in July.
articles.body:
A small power plant in the UK was shut down during a cyber attack.

The government said that at no point was there a risk to the UK's energy system, but the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has contacted power companies to advise them about the risk of cyber attacks.

The Telegraph reported that the attack, which took place last month, was carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime.

For security reasons, neither the government nor the National Cyber Security Centre, which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, would give further details of the site affected. However this was not an attack on an essential service such as a large power station.

According to the Telegraph, the power plant was shut down for four days.

DESNZ said the incident had affected a small-scale generator and at no point had there been a risk to the wider energy system.

The UK's power network has a number of smaller gas generators which provide short-term power when needed.

Protecting the country's supplies is a key challenge for the government. It is updating its regulations for cyber security, and working on a new energy resilience strategy for later this year.

Iran has long been regarded as a capable cyber power but while the Western cyber-security world is braced for attacks either from the state or hackers linked to the state as a result of its conflict with the US this year, there has been little activity so far.

What role has cyber warfare played in Iran?

Did Iran hack water systems in at least seven US states?

articles.title: Move to honour Channel Island journalists who resisted occupation
articles.summary: A commemoration is planned to journalists who resisted Nazi occupation during World War Two.
articles.body:
A memorial is planned to Channel Islands journalists who resisted Nazi occupation during World War Two.

The journalists included Joseph Gillingham and Joseph Tierney who were arrested, deported and died in prison for sharing news heard on banned radios and Frank Falla, who survived imprisonment and whose book The Silent War tells how islanders outmanoeuvred censorship.

The appeal by the Chartered Institute of Journalists for a plaque, in the journalists' church St Bride's in Fleet Street, London, has been led by historian Timothy Crook and has already reached its £1,000 target.

Crook said a "memorial can contribute to the restoration of a missing chapter of British journalistic history".

German armed forces occupied the Channel Islands from June 1940 until May 1945. While the islands' civil governments remained in place under German oversight, laws were introduced to confiscate and ban radios, enforce curfews and made everyone carry ID cards.

Crook said: "The memorial plaque intends to pay tribute to the people who spread news during the occupation by illegally listening to the BBC news having retained their radio sets after the order for their confiscation in June 1942.

"They distributed the BBC news they heard verbally or through clandestine news sheets.

"Many were not journalists before the occupation, but they certainly became courageous journalists during the occupation by disseminating the BBC news in these ways."

Institute president Gerald Bowey said donations received meant there could be a commemoration "to acknowledge the outstanding efforts and bravery of Channel Islands residents and journalists to resist censorship and keep the news flowing".

What happened in the Channel Islands during WW2?

The concrete reminders of five years of occupation

The appeal follows a talk to the institute by Cambridge University academic Gilly Carr, who spent a decade searching archives around the world to uncover information about the fate of Joe Gillingham from Guernsey and Joe Tierney from Jersey.

Gillingham was one of five members of the Guernsey Underground News Service (GUNS) who were deported and imprisoned for wireless offences and secretly spreading news.

GUNS was a loose collection of people who secretly listened to the BBC news, wrote it down and shared it with other islanders.

Often the news would contradict that put out through island newspapers, which were only allowed to carry war news provided and approved by the German authorities.

Carr's research resulted in the 2016 BBC documentary Finding Our Fathers , which followed the discovery of where Gillingham and Tierney had been buried in Europe.

Both men were crammed into cattle trucks and sent to prisons in the heart of Nazi Germany but their fates remained a mystery for 70 years.

Carr took the daughters of Gillingham and Tierney to Europe to retrace their fathers' steps in the hope of finding clues and eventually found their graves.

The St Bride's memorial could help extend Frank Falla's own campaign for recognitionl which involved writing letters to ministries and newspapers long after the war ended.

Falla fought for compensation for his fellow former political prisoners in the Channel Islands and, in 2010, his daughter gave Carr her father's extensive archives .

Carr, who described the files as "the single most important resistance archive ever to emerge from the Channel Islands" ensured it became available online.

The fundraisers said they hoped the memorial plaque would be placed in the south aisle of the church.

articles.title: Guinea rubbish landfill collapse kills 31 in Conakry
articles.summary: A mound of rubbish at a major waste site buried several homes in the capital, the government says.
articles.body:
At least 31 people have been killed after a mound of rubbish at a major waste site collapsed onto nearby homes in Guinea's capital Conakry, the government has said.

Another 22 people were injured, including six seriously, in the city's Dar-es-Salam area.

"Significant" resources and personnel - including the military - were deployed to search for survivors after the collapse at about 02:00 local time following heavy rain overnight, the government added in a statement.

One woman told local media her five children had died in the disaster. There are fears that the death toll will rise further.

Rescuers were later seen using excavators to comb through a mountain of scattered rubbish at the site as local residents gathered nearby.

One eyewitness said many people were buried when a second part of the site gave way.

"People tried to come to the rescue [after the first section collapsed]... They came running and climbed onto the refuse to see if anyone was there," Robert Kamano Sâa told the Associated Press.

"That was when the second section collapsed in three successive stages, cascading down. And that is what poured onto the people."

Guinea's Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah has visited the scene to assess the situation and oversee the search efforts.

Mamadouba Bangoura, who lost his house in the collapse, said he and his family were woken up by the "loud noise" of the first wave of rubbish, which did not reach them.

"[Then] the second wave came. That is what knocked over - pushed the house - and it fell," he told Reuters news agency.

"There were a lot of people [buried]... It is very, very difficult to talk about it because seeing a human being lose their life like that is pathetic, it is so painful."

Neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had earlier told the AFP news agency that he feared there would be a heavy death toll.

"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said.

Visiting the injured in hospital, Health Minister Khaïté Sall said they would get free medical care, while assuring families of government support.

Guinea has experienced similar landslide tragedies before, with 10 people being killed at the same site in 2017.

The government had recently ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.

Guinea's opposition figure and former Prime Minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident "a tragedy that plunges us into dismay".

"This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the landfill had been announced for this Sunday, 23 August", he said.

Rescue teams are continuing to search through the waste for others trapped underneath.

articles.title: Hampshire car wash 'worried' about possible business water use ban
articles.summary: Owners of a car wash are "worried" about the impact a water ban could have on its business and customers.
articles.body:
Operators of a car wash have said it will have to "close up" if further drought restrictions are approved.

Klodian Ferati from Pinkmead Car Wash in Botley, Hampshire, is "worried" about the potential impact a Non-Essential Use Ban (NEUB) could have on its staff, jobs and customers if approved.

Southern Water has applied to the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) for a Drought Order and NEUB , which could prevent businesses from using water.

The Environment Agency declared more than half of England in drought, and said as a precautionary measure the ban could be implemented to "protect water supplies and the environment".

Ferati said if it does come into effect the business "would close up completely because without water we can't actually do anything".

Pinkmead Car Wash was set up in 15 years ago, by manager Ferati and his family, because of their love for cars.

He said: "As a family, we love cars. We've always had cars and, you know, loved washing them at home.

"It will impact us a lot, even the business and the workers, because the business has rent to pay, has bills to pay, and the workers, they rely on this job. They have no other income.

"We could still do just the hoovering on the inside of the cars, but most of the customers, they're going to want their cars washed on the outside."

Klodian understands the need for the ban but hopes there can be a solution that means the business doesn't have to close: "We completely understand that Southern Water is short on water.

"But I think it's a great idea to work together and basically just come to a conclusion where we could, you know, use less water than before, and basically just carry on working."

A spokesperson for Southern Water, said: "These are precautionary measures and making an application does not mean they will be introduced.

"However, we must follow the regulatory process to protect water supplies and the environment if dry conditions persist."

The spokesperson said the company was "doing everything possible to protect water supplies" and had reduced leakage by around 25% over the past two years.

They added that the company was taking action as protecting the River Test remains one of its "highest priorities".

What activities will the possible ban affect?

Hampshire and the Isle of Wight were amongst seven English regions declared to be in drought conditions, last month.

According to water regulator Ofwat, while hosepipe bans mainly stop households from using a hose to water their garden, fill a paddling pool or wash their car, NEUBs specifically target businesses.

If the ban comes into force, the activities businesses must stop using water for would include filling or maintaining a non-domestic swimming pool, paddling pool or pond, operating a mechanical vehicle washer and cleaning any vehicle or non-domestic premises.

articles.title: A landslide at a landfill in the capital of Guinea kills 30 people, officials say
articles.summary: A mountainous heap of refuse collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea ‘s capital of Conakry early Sunday, killing 30 people, according to the central government.
articles.body: CONAKRY, Guinea — A mountainous heap of refuse collapsed at the largest landfill in Guinea’s capital of Conakry early Sunday, killing 30 people, according to the central government. Authorities said that heavy rains, which started around 2 a.m., washed over the refuse at Dar Es Salam — the largest landfill in Conakry — and triggered a landslide that buried nearby shacks. A search and rescue operation was underway to find survivors. Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed. The site, an open-air waste dump that is the largest in the city, had been designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion. Locals living around the landfill had been given eviction notices, which forced many to leave the area, but many others were still around at the time of the disaster, according to authorities. “We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere,” Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene. Guinea is mineral-rich with huge deposits of bauxite — the largest in the world — and also has iron ore, gold, diamonds and minerals. However, according to the World Bank, 43.7% of the population lives below the national poverty line.

Locals living around the landfill had been given eviction notices, which forced many to leave the area, but many others were still around at the time of the disaster, according to authorities. “We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere,” Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene. Guinea is mineral-rich with huge deposits of bauxite — the largest in the world — and also has iron ore, gold, diamonds and minerals. However, according to the World Bank, 43.7% of the population lives below the national poverty line.

articles.title: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of  2027 Eurovision Song Contest
articles.summary: It says contest can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.
articles.body:
Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, saying that the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.

In a statement released on Monday, the broadcaster said the decision was due to a lack of clarity from organisers - the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) - over assessing which countries could compete.

Avrotros added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."

Earlier this month, the EBU updated its rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. But Avrotros said those changes "do not provide sufficient confidence that ‌the ⁠independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".

The broadcaster's withdrawal from next year's contest in Burgas, Bulgaria, does not necessarily rule out Dutch participation.

Another public broadcaster could potentially take it on as the country has several.

Avrotros pulled out of this year's event in Vienna, Austria, which the Netherlands also boycotted after Israel were allowed to compete.

Only Ireland - who also pulled out of this year's event - and Sweden have won Eurovision more than the Netherlands.

Martin Green, director of the contest, said in a statement that the EBU regretted Avrotros's decision but respected its views.

"We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organisation for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest."

Taco Zimmerman, director general of Avrotos, said the Eurovision Song Contest "was originally created to bring people and countries together" but was now "a platform for division".

He said: "It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character.

"The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division. As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values."

He added: "They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts. That is painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the contest again next year."

Green, however, stated that the contest "has always been a place to bring people together, celebrate diverse communities, and show that a better world is possible even in the most difficult times".

The NPO said it was "very sorry" to hear that one of its broadcasters had pulled out of Eurovision again, but added that "we respect Avrotros's decision".

"We also recognise that the geopolitical tensions are having a divisive effect," it responded.

"That's why this hasn't been an easy decision for our colleagues. We will reflect on the upcoming edition and will come back to this at the right moment."

The organisation concluded it was "too early to comment on the next steps at this point" and that its members were "currently deliberating on that".

The recent amendment to the rules, that mean a country involved in an armed military conflict can't host the next contest if it wins, was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026.

It stated that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain, Ireland and the Netherlands.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

articles.title: Netherlands: Sixteen injured as coach carrying German students and van collide
articles.summary: Eight people, including the driver of a delivery van, are seriously hurt, police say.
articles.body:
Sixteen people have been injured as a coach carrying German high-school students collided with a delivery van in the eastern Netherlands, Dutch police have said.

Eight people including the van driver were seriously hurt, while the remainder suffered minor injuries, the police department of the Gelderland region said. All were taken to hospital, it added.

The cause of the accident, near Wezep, to the east of Amsterdam, is under investigation. It is unclear how many of the wounded were students.

More than 50 students and four teachers were on the coach travelling to Paris from a school in the northern German town of Schönberg, according to a notice on its website.

The students belonged to two grade 12 classes - typically for those aged 17 to 18 years old - it added.

The school said there had been no reports of life-threatening injuries and that all of those involved were receiving comprehensive medical care.

Police said they received a report of a serious accident on the A28 near Wezep at around time 04:20 local time (02:20 GMT) on Monday.

The coach collided with a delivery van, crashed through the guardrail, and overturned onto its side, according to Dutch and German media, citing local police.

The A28 highway remains closed in both directions following the accident.

articles.title: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board
articles.summary: Last year the organisation African Parks  admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.
